title: Galileo - Reservation Playbook, Burst Strategy & VPC Considerations
summary: Discovery focused on reserved GPU sizing, isolation levels for regulated workloads, burst capacity mechanics, and networking (VPC) needs. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot with a scoped benchmark and security docs to be shared.
next_steps: Redwood to share Dedicated reservation playbook + sample pricing by 2025-12-12
Customer to provide 1-week production trace and peak QPS by 2025-12-15
Schedule pilot kick-off (48-hour benchmark) week of 2025-12-22
action_items: Sophie Chen - Send dedicated_reservation_playbook.pdf and security_whitepaper.pdf - due 2025-12-12
Luis Ortega - Share 7-day tokenized traffic trace and 95th/99th percentile latencies - due 2025-12-15
Marco Alvarez - Draft pilot plan and benchmark script (load, model variants, failure scenarios) - due 2025-12-18
Tom Reynolds - Confirm procurement timeline and PO requirements - due 2025-12-19
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-10 16:00 PST | Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Alvarez (Redwood SE), Jared Bloom (Redwood CSM), Priya Nair (Galileo Head of Infra), Luis Ortega (ML Platform Lead), Dr. Ellen Park (CTO), Tom Reynolds (Procurement)

[00:00] Sophie Chen: Hey everyone. Thanks for carving time—this is Sophie on the Redwood side. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Priya Nair: Priya here. Hi.
[00:15] Luis Ortega: Luis, hi.
[00:17] Dr. Ellen Park: Ellen, good afternoon.
[00:20] Tom Reynolds: Tom from procurement.
[00:24] Marco Alvarez: Marco, SE. Jared on mute joining.
[00:28] Jared Bloom: Hey all.

[01:02] Sophie Chen: Cool. Goal for today: align on Galileo's expected utilization pattern for inference, isolation needs for regulated data, and an initial reserved GPU sizing + burst strategy. We can also hit networking and security items. Feel free to interrupt.

[01:35] Luis Ortega: To start, quick context. We run multiple low-latency chat endpoints and some batch embed jobs overnight. Peak real-time qps spikes 2,000 rps across several models; baseline is usually 300–400. We're evaluating Hosted vs Redwood Dedicated vs Private. Main ask: predictable cost and guaranteed isolation for PHI-ish customers.

[02:10] Sophie Chen: Helpful. When you say PHI-ish, can you say more about the controls you need? Is it full on-prem or VPC with KMS?

[02:28] Priya Nair: We need dedicated tenancy for some customers. VPC-only peering is preferred; also KMS integration and audit logs for any decryption. SOC 2 is required and we need proof of key rotation policies. Ideally air-gap later for a subset.

[02:55] Marco Alvarez: OK, so Dedicated with VPC and optional on-prem later maps cleanly. For reserved GPU sizing, do you have token- or concurrency-based metrics? Also what model variants are in play—Llama2-ish 7B quantized or 13B float?

[03:20] Luis Ortega: Mostly a mix. For prod chat we use a trimmed 13B quantized for latency; we have a small set of 70B experiments. Embeddings use a compact embed model. Tokenization distribution: median request 120 tokens, 95th is ~900 tokens for long context.

[03:50] Sophie Chen: Got it. So the working sizing assumption is sustained baseline around 300–400 rps, with 2k spikes. We typically size reserved pools to handle baseline plus a cushion, then configure burst capacity for spikes. For example, a pool sized for 500 rps sustained and a burst bucket that can absorb short 2k spikes for X minutes.

[04:18] Luis Ortega: How does Redwood charge for burst? Are we billed the same as reserved or higher rates?

[04:27] Sophie Chen: Burst is billed differently depending on config—there's a reserved hourly commitment and burst is pay-as-used at a premium, or you can purchase a burst credit bucket as part of the contract which is discounted. We'll send pricing matrix; Marco can show the math later in the pilot.

[05:05] Marco Alvarez: From an ops standpoint, burst uses a soft overcommit on available capacity in supported zones; if the dedicated pool saturates, traffic routes to compatible model variants or to hosted fallbacks depending on policy. We also support local autoscale with a cooldown and a fast-path for pre-warmed instances. We need to clarify failover SLAs for your team.

[05:47] Dr. Ellen Park: Fallbacks are OK so long as we control which customers are allowed to go to hosted in an emergency. Some of these customers require data residency guarantees.

[06:05] Soph ie Chen: Absolutely. You can pin a tenant routing policy to never fall back for certain customer IDs, or only fall back to Private in-region deployments. There was a slight audio glitch here.

[06:30] Priya Nair: About isolation—do you do GPU-level vs node-level tenancy? We want hardware isolation for specific regulated tenants.

[06:45] Marco Alvarez: Redwood supports node-level and physical GPU pool isolation. We can set up a dedicated host group where only your namespaces run. That meets typical regulatory requirements; for full physical airtightness we offer on-prem packaging too. Note: physical GPU tenancy sometimes increases provisioning lead time.

[07:20] Luis Ortega: Lead time—how long are we talking? We have a Q1 production target.

[07:28] Marco Alvarez: If you need physical-host dedicated racks in a zone, plan for 6–10 weeks for procurement and testing; reserved capacity in cloud regions is faster—usually 2–3 weeks depending on quota and capacity.

[07:52] Tom Reynolds: Procurement question: are there minimum contract lengths for reserved pools?

[07:58] Sophie Chen: Standard is 12 months for discounted reserved capacity but we can be flexible—9 or 6 months at tiered pricing, and pilot months can be month-to-month. We'll capture options in the quote.

[08:28] Luis Ortega: For burst, what's the technical trigger? Do we define QPS thresholds, and is there a token-based gating?

[08:40] Marco Alvarez: You can set a policy by concurrent requests, qps, or token throughput. We also allow traffic classing: high-priority vs best-effort lanes. High-priority never spills to hosted unless explicitly allowed. The KV cache—sorry K V cash in transcript—will help reduce cold token costs for repeated prompts.

[09:10] Priya Nair: About KV cache—does Redwood's KV cache persist across restarts and is it compatible with stateful chat? We have long conversations where prefix cache matters.

[09:27] Marco Alvarez: Yes, the prefix/KV cache is preserved in-memory for warm instances and we offer a persistent LRU-backed option for longer-term caching. There's a tradeoff on mem footprint vs warm hit rate that we'll quantify in the pilot.

[09:55] Luis Ortega: Latency targets—our SLO is 150ms p50 and 350ms p95 for standard chat requests. Can Redwood Dedicated meet that with quantized 13B?

[10:12] Marco Alvarez: In most cases yes—13B quantized on A100/P4 class nodes matches those SLOs for your token distributions. For 70B we recommend autoscale and heavier batching assumptions, which can raise tail latency. We'll include a latency-cost table.

[10:40] Sophie Chen: Quick clarification on benchmarking: for the pilot we recommend your production trace replayed across three model variants (13B q, 13B float, 70B quant) with a mix of short and long contexts. That will show us sustained utilization and tail behavior.

[11:10] Dr. Ellen Park: What about networking—VPC peering, egress control, and private control plane? We can't have control plane data traverse public internet for these tenants.

[11:28] Marco Alvarez: You can choose a private control plane with VPC peering and route control plane traffic over peered networks. For egress we support strict egress rules and NAT-less setups in some clouds, and we integrate with customer KMS, so keys never leave your account. A note: some telemetry/observability requires an opt-in agent that sends metrics; for regulated tenants that can be disabled and logs exported to your S3/GCS bucket.

[12:05] Priya Nair: SSO and audit—SAML or OIDC? Role-based access?

[12:12] Sophie Chen: We support SAML 2.0, OIDC, and granular RBAC. Audit logs are retained per configuration; we can push to your SIEM via secure delivery.

[12:40] Luis Ortega: Any gotchas with quantization and accuracy? We run quality-sensitive prompts where hallucination risk is a concern.

[12:52] Marco Alvarez: Quantization reduces memory/cost but can slightly affect accuracy in edge cases. Redwood Optimize provides quantization profiles per model/workload and we can run quality regressions in the pilot. We also support fallbacks to a higher-precision variant if a regression is detected.

[13:20] Tom Reynolds: On price predictability—if we hit sustained higher utilization mid-quarter, do you allow top-ups to the reserved pool?

[13:30] Sophie Chen: Yes—contracts include an option to add capacity midterm with pro-rated pricing. There are also burst credit buckets for short spikes to avoid immediate commitment.

[14:00] Priya Nair: Data residency—some EU customers must stay in-region. Can Dedicated be region-locked?

[14:08] Marco Alvarez: Yes. We can provision reserved pools in specific regions and configure routing to keep requests within region boundaries. For GDPR/Schengen requirements we'll add data residency clauses in the contract.

[14:30] Luis Ortega: Let's talk about failure scenarios. Suppose a zone loses capacity—how is traffic redistributed?

[14:40] Marco Alvarez: Smart routing will prefer compatible variants in other regions if policy allows; alternatively, traffic can be queued or we can fall back to hosted endpoints if allowed. We can also pre-warm cross-region pools for critical tenants. We'll design RTO/RPO targets with you in the pilot.

[15:05] Dr. Ellen Park: We want a runbook for outage scenarios and a 48-hour failover drill. Can Redwood participate?

[15:12] Marco Alvarez: Absolutely — we recommend a joint runbook and a scheduled failover test during the pilot.

[16:00] Sophie Chen: On pricing detail we'll send a couple of scenarios: 1) baseline reserved pool with burst credits, 2) reserved pool + dedicated host group for regulated tenants, and 3) hybrid with Private control plane.

[16:25] Luis Ortega: For the pilot scope—how much reserved capacity do you recommend as a starting point?

[16:33] Marco Alvarez: Given your numbers, start with a pool sized for 600 rps sustained on 13B quant, with a 5k token burst bucket to cover short 2k spikes for up to 10 minutes. That maps to roughly N GPUs depending on packing; we'll produce the exact GPU count once we run your trace.

[17:02] Priya Nair: Any network requirements on our side for peering? IP ranges, firewall exceptions?

[17:09] Marco Alvarez: We'll request a small set of CIDR ranges for peering, a couple of firewall ports for control plane' and an S3/GCS destination for logs. We'll provide a checklist.

[17:35] Sophie Chen: I'll attach the checklist and the dedicated_reservation_playbook after the call.

[18:00] Luis Ortega: A few practical things—token accounting: do you meter on model tokens in/out or full prompt+response?

[18:12] Sophie Chen: We meter total tokens processed (prompt + generated). You can get per-route breakdowns in the console.

[18:30] Tom Reynolds: For contract negotiation, are there penalties for early termination?

[18:36] Sophie Chen: Typically yes for deeply discounted multi-month commitments, but pilots and short introductory terms can be structured to be low friction. We'll include a few standard options.

[19:05] Priya Nair: Any compliance docs we should review? SOC 2, ISO 27001, penetration test report?

[19:14] Sophie Chen: We'll send our SOC 2 Type II, ISO summary, and a redacted pentest report. For KMS integration we'll include the key handling whitepaper.

[19:45] Luis Ortega: On monitoring, can we get token-level cost and latency breakdown per tenant?

[19:54] Marco Alvarez: Yes, the console exposes per-route/per-tenant telemetry and cost attribution. You can also pipe metrics into your observability stack.

[20:20] Dr. Ellen Park: Let's lock the pilot goals: validate latency SLOs p50/p95, surface cost per 1M tokens across workload mixes, and test failover/runbook.

[20:34] Sophie Chen: Agreed. We'll put that in the pilot charter.

[21:00] Tom Reynolds: Timing on the pilot contract—what's typical?

[21:05] Sophie Chen: 30–60 days pilot with a focused benchmark is common. We'll scope it for 2 weeks of load replay plus a 48-hour failover drill.

[21:30] Luis Ortega: Ok good. Any other blockers from our side?

[21:35] Priya Nair: We need legal to review the data processing annex and ensure KMS terms are acceptable.

[21:40] Tom Reynolds: Yup procurement will review.

[22:00] Sophie Chen: Great. Quick recap and next steps: I'll send the playbook and security artifacts by Friday 2025-12-12. Luis will share the 7-day trace by Monday the 15th. Marco will prepare the pilot plan by the 18th. We'll tentatively schedule pilot kickoff the week of 2025-12-22.

[22:30] Luis Ortega: Sounds good.

[22:35] Dr. Ellen Park: Thanks all.

[22:40] Sophie Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links.

[22:50] Meeting end.
